title: Timeout
explain: A timeout is a decision to stop waiting, not a verdict. After one I do not know whether the other side did nothing, is still working, or finished and the reply was lost. So I treat the outcome as unknown, make the operation safe to repeat, and use three separate clocks: connect, request, and an end-to-end deadline.
model:
Three clocks, three jobs:

| Clock | Covers | Rule of thumb |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Connect timeout** | TCP/TLS handshake | short, hundreds of ms to ~1 s: an unreachable host is cheap to abandon |
| **Request (read) timeout** | waiting for the response, or between bytes | a bit above the dependency's p99 to p99.9, never the library default of 30 s or infinite |
| **End-to-end deadline** | the whole user request | one absolute time passed down the chain |

Each hop gets `deadline - now - margin`, so inner timeouts are always shorter than outer ones. If the budget is gone, fail fast without calling.

A timeout is only half a design: it must be paired with a next step, which is a [retry](#/sd/f/retry) inside a budget, a [circuit breaker](#/sd/f/circuit-breaker), or a fallback. Where the timer lives and who judges expiry is [time-box patterns](#/sd/f/time-box-patterns).

No timeout means a stuck call holds a thread, connection and memory forever, and a slow dependency becomes your outage.

details.q: The call timed out at 2.0 s but the provider finished the charge at 2.3 s. What do you conclude?
details.a: That the outcome is unknown. Showing failure and sending a fresh request risks charging twice. Retry or reconcile with the same [idempotency key](#/sd/f/idempotency) so the original outcome is returned.

details.q: The peer accepts the connection but never writes a byte. Client has a 1 s connect timeout only. What happens?
details.a: The client blocks as long as the peer keeps the socket open. The connect timeout stops mattering once the handshake completes; only a request/read timeout can fire.

details.q: A gateway sets a 3,000 ms deadline; A uses 400 ms, B uses 900 ms. What timeout does B give its database call with a 100 ms margin?
details.a: 3000 - 400 - 900 = 1700 ms remaining, minus the 100 ms margin is 1600 ms. If the budget is zero or negative, fail fast without making the call.

details.q: A calls B with a 1 s timeout and B calls C with 5 s. C takes 4 s. What is the problem?
details.a: A leaves at 1 s but B keeps waiting on C until 4 s: orphaned work still consuming B and C capacity. Derive inner timeouts from a propagated deadline so they are shorter than the caller's remaining time.

details.q: Where do you set the request timeout?
details.a: A little above the dependency's p99 to p99.9 latency. At the median you fail many healthy requests; far above the tail it protects nothing.

details.q: What do you do right after a timeout?
details.a: Cancel the abandoned call so it stops consuming resources, treat the state as unknown, then decide using the remaining budget: retry, fallback, or fail. A retry that ignores the deadline stretches latency past what the user will wait for.

prompts.q: Explain what a timeout does and does not tell you, and what you do next.
points: It only means we stopped waiting
Outcome unknown: not done, still running, or done and reply lost
Pair with retry budget, breaker or fallback

prompts.q: Describe the three timeouts you would configure on an outbound HTTP call.
points: End-to-end deadline for the whole request
Each hop uses remaining time minus margin

prompts.q: Walk through why inner timeouts must be shorter than outer ones.
points: Caller leaves while callee still works: orphan work
